1.note: חֲלִיצוֹת is read as festal garments, like מַחֲלָצוֹת (Isa 3:22, Zech 3:4). In 2 Sam 2:21 the word means armor stripped from the slain.

2.he: אֶבְנֶה אֲנִי בִּית אֶחָד וְאֲיַסֵּד הַבִּנְיָן.
2.note: בַּיִת is both "house" and "line of verse", so the verse is "built". The rules of the contest: the young man says the first half (or line), the old man completes it.

3.note: שְׁחָרִים is read as "dawns": the white page is the dawn, the ink a row of darkness on it. The word can also be heard as "blackness" (שָׁחֹר), "embroiders in black".

4.note: Pun: הָאֱמוּנָה (faith) and אֲמוּנָה (nursed, reared, as Lam 4:5 הָאֱמֻנִים, Esth 2:20 בְאָמְנָה). A letter is reared in trust: it keeps its secrets.

5.note: Ps 92:6 "Your thoughts are very deep", said of God. Here מַחְשָׁבוֹת is probably "designs, craftsmanship" (as in Exod 35:32 לַחְשֹׁב מַחֲשָׁבֹת), the work of the mail.

6.note: Pun: פְּתוּחוֹת (open) and פִּתּוּחֵי (engravings, Exod 28:11). The doors of the "tower" are shut, but its carved frames are full of openings: the holes between the rings. The sense is uncertain.

7.note: The image is unclear: perhaps the rough, ridged hide of a camel. Repeated in the old man's verse below.

8.note: Read with Isa 9:1 "the people who walk in darkness" and Ps 34:6 "they looked to him and were radiant" (וְנָהָרוּ). Perhaps of the horse's white blaze or its gleaming coat. Uncertain.

9.note: Pun: שׂוֹרֵק (the choice vine, Isa 5:2; Gen 49:11 שֹׂרֵקָה) and שׁוֹרֵק (whistles, summons, as Isa 5:26 וְשָׁרַק לוֹ). Wine calls joys to it.

10.note: The text prints וְתוֹםֵשׂ, apparently a misprint for וְתוֹפֵשׂ "and seizes" (ם for פ). Translated as וְתוֹפֵשׂ; the Hebrew is not changed. The two arrows are the talons.

11.note: The dark cloud is a Cushite: his rage is the thunder, his laughter (white teeth) the flash.

12.note: Wordplay: יוֹסִיף (adds, goes on) and יָסוּף (comes to an end); compare Deut 5:19 וְלֹא יָסָף. "Pent-up" renders אָסוּף "gathered".

13.note: פַּעַם read as "foot" (as Song 7:2 פְעָמַיִךְ): the round body of the lyre and its neck, or the lyre held against the player's thigh. In the next lines פַּעַם returns as "anvil" (Isa 41:7 הוֹלֵם פָּעַם). Uncertain.

14.note: The rhyme word גֻּלָּה is used twice: a round bowl (Eccl 12:6 גֻּלַּת הַזָּהָב) and a spring or pool (Josh 15:19 גֻּלֹּת מָיִם). The subject is the water-wheel (noria).

15.he: אַחַר גְּדוּד הָאֹפֶל דּוֹלֵק. וְחִצָּיו לְהַשְׁמִיד דּוֹלֵק.
15.note: The rhyme word דּוֹלֵק is used three times: "burning", "hotly pursuing" (Gen 31:36 דָלַקְתָּ אַחֲרָי), and "kindling" its arrows (Ps 7:14 חִצָּיו לְדֹלְקִים יִפְעָל).

16.note: תַּרְשִׁישׁ is a precious stone (Exod 28:20), here also the sea, which the medieval poets call by the name of Tarshish. The moon's path is gold set on the stone, or on the sea.

17.note: שָׂרִיג is a tendril or shoot (Gen 40:10); אֶזְרָח a native tree (Ps 37:35 כְּאֶזְרָח רַעֲנָן). A young plant of the soil: the old man praises the youth's freshness.

18.note: תְּעוּדָה is "testimony, record" (Isa 8:16, 20). Probably the heads of the writings or of the learned. The sense is uncertain.

19.note: Pun on the hero's name: חֶבֶר (Ḥever) and אֲחַבֵּר (I join together, I compose). This is the gate's recognition scene.

20.note: Rhyme and pun: בִּשְׁמוֹ (by his name), line before, and בָּשְׂמוֹ (his spice).

21.note: Prov 25:13 "a faithful envoy". צִיר also means a pang (1 Sam 4:19), so his wandering left both a messenger of him and a pain in the narrator's heart.
